text: Nearly every team has built a dashboard with a big green uptime percentage at the top, and it feels reassuring right up until an incident, when it turns out to be nearly useless. That's the gap this lesson closes — the difference between a metric that looks calm in a status meeting and one that actually tells you a user is being hurt right now.

Uptime by health-check definition and uptime as users experience it are not the same number — a process can answer its health check while a real request times out against a saturated dependency behind it. Raw request count has the same blind spot in the other direction: a flat, healthy traffic line says nothing about success rate or latency. And averages are the quietest trap, because a handful of badly affected requests barely moves a mean calculated across everything else that's working fine.

So what should a dashboard be built around instead? Google's SRE book names four golden signals — latency, traffic, errors, and saturation — as the real starting checklist. Two shorthand methods build on the same idea: RED, for Rate, Errors, and Duration, fits anything that serves requests, like an API. USE, for Utilization, Saturation, and Errors, fits infrastructure like a database or a queue. Neither is exotic tooling — it's a disciplined list of what to put on a panel before reaching for whatever metric already exists.

Here's the query that belongs on that dashboard: p99 latency per route, using histogram_quantile over a rate of a duration histogram, grouped by both the latency bucket and the route. That one query encodes the whole lesson — percentile instead of average, broken down by dimension instead of aggregated into one line.

A real worked example makes this concrete. A checkout API's average response time looked normal during an incident where a subset of users couldn't check out — one backend instance behind the load balancer had a slow disk, serving every third request in eight seconds instead of eighty milliseconds. Averaged across every instance, that barely moved the mean. The p99 line would have jumped immediately, because the 99th percentile is built to expose a problem hurting a minority of requests badly, not one spread evenly across all of them.

That's the concrete takeaway to carry into the next lesson: percentiles instead of averages for latency, and panels broken down per endpoint, per backend instance, and per region, because an aggregate is precisely what hides a localized failure. Next, you'll build dashboards around exactly these signals for real, in Grafana, pulling data from both Azure Monitor and CloudWatch side by side.
